lines: +# Separate workflow connection sharing from grant management and use

+An Elsa 3 workflow can use a named connection through a durable grant tied to its instance, logical binding, connection and binding revision. The grant manager already requires an authenticated actor and a host grant-management policy, and each execution rechecks the stored grant. Grant management alone did not express whether that actor was allowed to **share this particular connection with this workflow**. General connection management and metadata inspection are separate decisions.

+Issuing a workflow-use grant requires two independent host decisions: `IConnectionCredentialGrantManagementAuthorizer` for the grant operation and `IConnectionCredentialShareAuthorizer` for the exact tenant, configured environment, workflow instance, binding, connection and binding revision. The sharing policy defaults to deny when the host has not registered an implementation. The grant manager derives this scope from the trusted tenant accessor, configured environment and persisted binding; workflow-authored input cannot provide it. A denied decision writes no grant.

+Withdrawal requires grant-management authorization and the expected grant revision, but does not require continuing share permission. This lets an administrator revoke an existing share after the right to create new shares has been removed. The existing durable grant stays the runtime entitlement: every subsequent credential resolution reloads its active state, binding revision and connection status, alongside the host's separate binding-use policy. A withdrawal cannot cancel a provider call that was already admitted.

+This is **workflow-instance sharing**, not general person/team delegation. No new credential store, plaintext API, package identity, or persisted grant schema is introduced. Hosts that opt into workflow grants must register both host policies to issue them; the default remains deny. Existing non-sharing connection use and metadata inspection do not gain access through a grant.

+The two decisions can be audited and tested independently. A host that previously provided only grant-management authorization will now fail closed at issuance until it explicitly supplies sharing policy. Revocation uses the existing grant's durable conditional update, so it is visible to later workers and persisted workflow resumes. Broader user/team sharing, provider-side consent delegation and user-facing Studio controls require separate design and are not inferred from this instance-scoped mechanism.

@@ -10,6 +10,7 @@ This guide records the boundaries and operational limits of the initial Core cre

- `IConnectionMetadataInspector` is a separate host-only read seam. The host configures `ConnectionInspectionOptions.EnvironmentId` and an `IConnectionUseAuthorizer` policy for human purpose `inspect:metadata`. Missing configuration or lifecycle persistence, unauthenticated actors, default/agnostic tenant context, or the default deny authorizer return no record. The service reads only in the ambient tenant and configured environment, then returns a fixed DTO with connection/provider/account identity, status and revision; secret names, generation IDs and credential operation state are omitted. Management or workflow-use permission alone does not imply inspection. No public HTTP endpoint or broad person/team sharing is installed. The durable workflow-use grant remains the only implemented sharing path and is scoped to one workflow instance and binding revision. See the [inspection decision](../../adr/2026-09-25-connection-metadata-inspection-boundary.md).

- Logical workflow bindings select a connection in the trusted tenant and configured integration environment; they do not grant use. Without a binding-store provider, the workflow adapter's default store returns no mappings and binding management/use fail closed. A host that provides a binding store must also configure lifecycle persistence and `IConnectionBackgroundUseService`; a valid mapping with that lifecycle path missing is a host configuration error and is not hidden as a normal unavailable result. A disconnect can race the binding store's active-state check and leave a stale mapping. Each resolve still passes through the lifecycle service, which rejects disconnected connections.

- `WorkflowCredentialUseGrantsFeature` is opt-in. It requires a durable Connections grant store and a separate host-provided `IConnectionCredentialGrantManagementAuthorizer`; its defaults deny grant management and return no grants. At use time, the grant check is mandatory in addition to any host `IConnectionCredentialBindingUseAuthorizer`; enabling grants never replaces a host's extra use restrictions. An authenticated actor may issue a grant only for the trusted tenant, configured environment, exact workflow instance and current active binding revision. Concurrent issuance for the same scope yields at most one grant; recognized PostgreSQL serialization conflicts return a controlled failed issuance. Withdrawing a grant uses a revision check and permanently disables that instance/binding pair; do not delete the row to reauthorize it. Use a new workflow instance until an explicit reissue policy is designed. Grant rows contain no Secrets values. Back up and restore these rows with bindings and connection state; SQLite and PostgreSQL grant migrations intentionally have no in-place `Down` path. After withdrawal, rebind, or disconnect, the next credential resolution fails closed, while a previously admitted provider call can still finish.

+- Issuing that exact-instance grant also requires the host's distinct `IConnectionCredentialShareAuthorizer`. Its request names the trusted tenant, configured environment, workflow instance, logical binding, connection and binding revision; the opt-in feature registers a deny-all default. Grant management alone cannot share a connection. Withdrawal still requires grant-management authorization and expected revision, but does not require continued sharing permission, so an existing share can be revoked after issue permission is removed. The stored grant is rechecked on each workflow use. This is workflow-instance sharing, not general user/team delegation; no public credential or broad share endpoint is enabled. See the [sharing decision](../../adr/2026-09-25-separate-workflow-connection-sharing-authorization.md).

- `ResolveForUseAsync` returns an access-only credential. Refresh tokens stay inside lifecycle/provider operations. Connection results, secret listings, and serialized access DTOs contain no token values. The generic Secrets resolver remains a trusted low-level API for unowned secrets and does not authorize an actor.

- Tenant, environment, connection, and generation identity are checked together on reads and mutations. Copying an environment's logical connection configuration does not copy its token generation or encryption key. Do not export or promote raw token material.

- Local disconnect, token-pair revocation, and installation uninstall are distinct authorized actions. Disconnect commits `Disconnected` and its completed local operation record in one SQLite-tested transaction; it does not imply remote revoke or uninstall. A token-revocation request must name a lifecycle-owned generation, and that generation stays pinned while the operation is unresolved. Installation uninstall uses provider-owned host credentials and stores no Connections generation reference. It must not silently fall back to the connection's OAuth token.

The API-key fixture creates encrypted managed Secrets generations and durable workflow-use grants through the real feature registrations. It proves that a replacement is published through lifecycle revision/fence checks, old generations can be retired, and a disconnected or out-of-scope connection cannot be resolved by the persisted workflow. Its marker is absent from the grant, raw persisted workflow data, reloaded workflow state, serialized workflow state, and captured host logs. Separate lifecycle tests cover concurrent replacement, stale-revision denial, local retirement/disconnect, and recovery after a lost staged-generation write. These are synthetic tests; no provider account or real API key is used.

+Grant issuance now checks the host's distinct workflow-instance sharing decision as well as grant-management authorization. The test host registers both policies explicitly; the feature's default sharing policy denies issuance. A focused unit case proves that grant management alone writes no share, that the share request carries the trusted tenant/environment and exact binding snapshot, and that a grant can still be withdrawn after sharing permission is removed. The persisted grant remains the use-time entitlement, so the next resolution after withdrawal fails closed. General person/team sharing and provider-side consent delegation are outside this contract.

The first host runs under tenant `tenant-a` and persists the workflow, bookmark, binding, and grant. The second host applies tenant routing from its trusted host context before loading the instance. Wrong-tenant routing cannot load the tenant-scoped instance. The environment comes from host configuration, never workflow input. This proves persisted resume through the real runtime client; it does not prove automatic routing by `RestartInterruptedWorkflowsTask`, a scheduler, or a queue consumer.

The runtime test checks the raw persisted workflow `Data` column, the reloaded workflow input, output, properties and incident messages, the same `IWorkflowStateSerializer` used by workflow-instance export, and captured host logs for the synthetic credential marker. Run the separate persisted two-host TestServer test with `dotnet test test/integration/Elsa.Connections.Credentials.Persistence.PostgreSql.IntegrationTests/Elsa.Connections.Credentials.Persistence.PostgreSql.IntegrationTests.csproj -f net10.0 -c Release --filter FullyQualifiedName~ExportAfterPersistedApiKeyWorkflowResume_RedactsCredentialFromAllOptionalSections`. On 2026-09-24, the filtered test passed (1/1, none skipped). It invokes single-instance HTTP GET and POST exports, then a bulk ZIP export containing two workflow instances, with bookmarks, activity execution logs, and workflow execution logs included. It scans every returned response and ZIP entry plus the raw persisted state for the API-key marker. The fixture uses SQLite and synthetic activity output; it does not establish redaction of an arbitrary secret deliberately written into a workflow log or validate a production provider. The granted call is already admitted once the resolver returns; a later withdrawal, rebind, or disconnect cannot retract an in-flight provider call. Lifecycle authorization and a final active-connection check remain separate boundaries.
